messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Vinh's Vigil

Vinh Nguyen was forty-eight years old when the tank ruptured. He had been servicing the HVAC system in the basement of the Riverside Chemical facility for nearly twenty years—a reliable technician, known for his precision and his quiet competence—when a coupling on an adjacent storage vessel failed catastrophically. The chemical release was sudden and suffocating; he remembered the acrid burn in his lungs, the way his vision blurred, the panic of not knowing what he had breathed in or what it might do to him. He stumbled upstairs, gasping, and the facility's emergency response team got him to the hospital where they pumped his stomach and ran tests. The doctors said he was fortunate—the exposure had been brief, the chemical a corrosive but not immediately lethal irritant. No permanent organ damage. He was discharged after three days with a prescription for an inhaler and instructions to follow up with occupational medicine.

But Vinh never went back to work at the facility. Four years have passed since that day, and he has cycled through a series of shorter-term HVAC jobs, always finding reasons to leave—a new building, a new company, never staying long enough to feel settled. His wife, Linh, says he is not the same man she married. He is fifty-two now, and his body has become a stranger to him, a thing that cannot be trusted to keep him safe. Even lying in bed at night, his muscles remain coiled, his breathing shallow and ready. He wakes sometimes in the dark convinced that something toxic is seeping under the bedroom door, that the walls themselves are poisoning the air.

What terrifies Vinh most is the conviction that danger is always present, waiting, invisible. When Linh tries to reassure him—when she says the house is safe, the air is clean, nothing bad is going to happen—he hears the words but cannot believe them. He has come to understand that his own senses cannot be trusted either. The chemical had no smell at first; how can he trust that he would know if it came again? This certainty that safety is an illusion has reshaped everything he does. He checks the doors and windows obsessively, five, six, seven times an evening, his hand on each lock, testing it, releasing it, testing again. He has installed additional locks on the bedroom door and the garage. He avoids being alone in any enclosed space—the bathroom, the basement, even a closet—because the thought of being trapped without an exit, without someone who might hear him if something goes wrong, sends his heart into an irregular rhythm. Linh has learned to leave the bathroom door open when she showers, knowing he will stand in the hallway, listening.

He has also stopped trying to relax. The first few months after the exposure, he attempted to follow his doctor's advice to manage stress—he tried sitting quietly, tried to meditate as Linh suggested—but the moment he began to slow his breathing and settle his body, a different kind of panic rose in him. Relaxation felt like lowering his guard, like inviting danger in. If he was not vigilant, not tense, not ready to react, then something would happen. He cannot afford to be calm. The tension in his shoulders and jaw has become permanent, a kind of armor. He avoids anything that might require him to be at ease—he turned down a promotion that would have meant sitting in an office, he stopped attending his nephew's soccer games because the bleachers felt too exposed and too crowded, he declined his brother's invitation to go fishing. Any situation that demands he be present without the ability to monitor threats feels unbearable. His current job, a contract position maintaining systems in a series of small office buildings, is tolerable only because he can move between spaces, can keep moving, can maintain the illusion of control. But even that is becoming harder. Last month, a client asked him to stay late to finish a repair, and Vinh found himself unable to comply. The building was emptying out, the lights in the hallway dimming, and the thought of being alone in that structure—even for another hour—made him dizzy with dread.

Linh finally insisted he see someone after she found him at three in the morning, standing in the kitchen with all the windows open despite the winter cold, convinced he could smell something acrid in the air. There was nothing there. There has been nothing there for four years. But Vinh has made an appointment with a therapist, though he is not certain what help could possibly look like. How do you convince your body that it is safe when you know, with absolute certainty, that it is not?

violation_explanations: The vignette describes Vinh's sense of threat (conviction that danger is always present, invisible threats, inability to trust his senses) and his maladaptive strategies (checking locks obsessively, avoiding enclosed spaces, maintaining tension, avoiding relaxation), but does not establish a clear causal relationship showing that his perceived threat directly drives or motivates his maladaptive coping behaviors. The strategies appear as parallel symptoms rather than as consequences of the threat perception.
